analysis.one_liner: Lets wheelchair and mobility-device owners and independent shops get the parts, manuals, and software needed to repair them.
analysis.headline: The Wheelchair Right to Repair Act was introduced in August 2025 and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it legal for owners and independent repair shops to bypass digital locks on motorized wheelchairs and similar devices in order to diagnose or fix them, and it would require the manufacturers to sell them the same manuals, diagnostic software, firmware, and parts they give their own authorized repair networks, on equal terms. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the requirement. Manufacturers would not have to hand over true trade secrets or sell parts that no longer exist, and they would not be liable for damage caused by an independent repair. The bill has not moved since it was referred to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use powered wheelchairs, scooters, and robotic walking devices — many of them disabled and on fixed incomes — gain the ability to fix their devices themselves or use any repair shop they choose, instead of relying on manufacturer-authorized networks that can be slow and expensive. Independent repair businesses gain legal access to the manuals, diagnostic software, and parts they need to compete with the manufacturers' own service channels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wheelchair users and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: It changes federal copyright law so that bypassing a digital lock to diagnose, maintain, or repair a powered wheelchair or exoskeleton is not illegal.

It requires manufacturers to sell or provide owners and independent repair shops the same parts, manuals, software, and diagnostic tools they give their own authorized repair networks, on equal terms.
It requires manufacturers to publish a standard request process, notify buyers of their rights, and let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of powered wheelchairs and mobility devices would bear the cost of sharing diagnostic software, documentation, and parts with independent shops and owners on terms equal to their authorized dealers, and would lose some control and revenue from their repair monopolies.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would have to hand over diagnostic software, firmware, and security-lock tools to independent shops, which they argue could raise device security and safety risks.

The bill shields manufacturers from liability for damage or injury caused by independent repairs, so a botched repair by a third party could leave a user with limited recourse against the manufacturer.
Enforcement depends on FTC action and state attorneys general; a user cannot sue on their own, so compliance would rely on agency willingness and capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: wheelchair users would gain the legal right and practical means to fix their own devices, cutting repair costs and downtime, and independent repair shops would gain access to parts, software, and documentation at no worse terms than authorized dealers. The costs are modest but real: manufacturers would have to share diagnostic software and tools they now keep exclusive, which they argue could weaken device security and their control of repair quality, and the bill as drafted relies on FTC enforcement that would depend on the agency's willingness to act. There is also an honest design question about whether repair providers can handle safety-critical powered equipment; the bill addresses this with a liability rule placing responsibility on the repairer, which protects manufacturers but shifts risk to device users. On balance, the repair-access gains outweigh the concerns for this narrow product category.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late August 2025 and sent to two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: H.R. 5039 was introduced in the House on August 26, 2025.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
The action history shows no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action since referral.
It has one cosponsor, a Democrat, in addition to sponsor Rep. Maxwell Frost.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet — the bill has simply gone nowhere. The status quo favors manufacturers, who keep exclusive control of wheelchair repair.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers keep their repair monopoly so far

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two named supporters are both Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored and no opponent has acted on the record yet, so the partisan shape is not established.

analysis.trajectory: Most right-to-repair bills introduced in Congress die in committee without a hearing or a vote, and a first-term bill with a single cosponsor facing two committee referrals has long odds. The best realistic near-term path is attention from committee hearings on manufacturer repair restrictions; passage this Congress is unlikely.
